title: Hardening, Transplant & Outdoor Establishment
summary: Plants moved from protected conditions into outdoor sun, wind, temperature swings, and lower humidity need an establishment period. Acclimation should be evaluated through plant response rather than a fixed number of days.
keyConcepts: Protected-grown leaves may be poorly acclimated to full solar and wind exposure
Root disturbance and atmospheric demand can compound transplant stress
Gradual exposure allows new growth to develop under the destination environment
Container root condition and soil moisture at transplant strongly influence establishment
measureObserve: Track exposure duration and weather during acclimation
Inspect midday leaf posture and recovery by evening
Check root-zone moisture before and after transplant
Record new-growth condition rather than judging recovery from old damaged leaves
commonMistakes: Moving plants directly from low light to full sun
Transplanting into dry soil and then trying to correct later
Interpreting temporary acclimation stress as a nutrient deficiency
Ignoring wind exposure during hardening

title: Frost, Heat & Seasonal Extremes
summary: Outdoor crops experience radiative cooling, frost pockets, heat waves, hot surfaces, and abrupt weather transitions. Risk depends on plant stage, local topography, soil and ground cover, wind, humidity, and duration of exposure.
keyConcepts: Low areas can accumulate colder air on calm nights
Soil moisture, texture, and ground cover change heat storage and nighttime release
Heat stress depends on radiation, leaf temperature, water supply, and air movement
Weather-station readings may not represent the crop microclimate
measureObserve: Record canopy-level minimum and maximum temperature
Identify low spots and exposed slopes
Measure or estimate leaf temperature during heat events
Inspect recovery after an extreme event before making unrelated corrections
commonMistakes: Using only regional forecast temperature
Assuming mulch always reduces frost risk
Increasing irrigation blindly during heat without checking root oxygen
Diagnosing weather injury as nutrition from appearance alone

title: Native Soil Testing & Amendment Decisions
summary: Outdoor soil decisions should start with physical and chemical evidence. Texture, structure, drainage, pH, salinity, organic matter, and nutrient tests answer different questions and should not be replaced by a generic amendment recipe.
keyConcepts: Soil texture and aggregation affect drainage, aeration, and water storage
Laboratory nutrient values depend on the extraction method used
pH influences chemical availability but does not diagnose every plant symptom
Adding amendments without a measured need can create excesses or imbalance
measureObserve: Collect a representative soil sample using a documented pattern
Record texture and infiltration separately from laboratory chemistry
Review pH, soluble salts or EC, organic matter, and nutrient results with the lab method
Retest after major changes when meaningful
commonMistakes: Testing one handful from an unusual spot
Treating bagged amendment instructions as a soil diagnosis
Adding lime or sulfur without measured pH context
Ignoring drainage because a nutrient test looks acceptable

title: Mulch, Groundcover & Soil-Surface Management
summary: The soil surface affects evaporation, temperature, weed competition, splash, traffic, and frost heat exchange. Mulch and groundcover can be useful, but their effects change with material, thickness, weather, and season.
keyConcepts: Mulch can reduce surface evaporation and splash
Organic surface layers can alter soil temperature and moisture patterns
Dense groundcover competes for water and can change nighttime heat exchange
Surface management also affects access for scouting and irrigation inspection
measureObserve: Check moisture beneath and beyond the mulch layer
Record soil temperature at comparable depths
Inspect for persistent saturation or pest shelter
Observe splash and erosion during heavy rain
commonMistakes: Assuming mulch is always beneficial in every season
Letting mulch contact stems continuously
Using surface appearance to infer deeper moisture
Ignoring groundcover water use
visualNeeds: Mulched versus bare soil water balance

title: Wildlife, Herbivory & Physical Protection
summary: Outdoor plant loss can come from browsing, digging, chewing, trampling, birds, rodents, or larger wildlife. Damage pattern and site evidence should guide exclusion rather than assuming every missing leaf is an insect problem.
keyConcepts: Different animals leave different feeding and movement evidence
Young plants can be disproportionately vulnerable
Physical barriers are usually more predictable than repellents alone
Protection should not block airflow, light, drainage, or routine inspection
measureObserve: Photograph tracks, droppings, bite patterns, or disturbed soil
Record time of day when damage appears
Inspect barrier gaps and digging points
Separate wildlife damage from insect chewing and mechanical breakage
commonMistakes: Applying insect treatments to vertebrate damage
Installing barriers that shade or restrict plants
Ignoring underground digging
Waiting for repeated losses before mapping entry routes

title: Pollen Drift & Outdoor Pollination Risk
summary: Airborne pollen can move beyond the source plant. Outdoor pollination risk depends on flowering synchrony, source abundance, wind and turbulence, distance, terrain, and local plantings; visual distance alone cannot guarantee isolation.
keyConcepts: Cannabis pollen can be transported by air
Risk is highest when viable pollen release overlaps receptive flowers
Wind direction changes over time
Physical distance lowers but does not make risk zero
measureObserve: Record nearby known pollen sources when possible
Track male or pollen-producing flower development
Document prevailing and event-specific wind direction
Inspect receptive flowers and later seed formation across the site
commonMistakes: Treating a single isolation distance as a guarantee
Ignoring neighboring volunteer or unmanaged plants
Using average wind direction instead of actual flowering-period conditions
Assuming absence of visible pollen means no exposure

title: Wildfire Smoke, Dust & Surface Contamination
summary: Outdoor foliage and flowers can collect ash, dust, soil particles, spray drift, and other airborne material. Visible residue should be documented as exposure evidence rather than assumed to be a disease or nutrient symptom.
keyConcepts: Particle deposition depends on source, wind, canopy position, and surface characteristics
Residues can interfere with visual pest and disease inspection
Flowers are difficult to clean without potentially changing quality or adding moisture
Exposure history matters for deciding whether testing or rejection is appropriate
measureObserve: Document air-quality or dust events and wind direction
Compare protected and exposed plant surfaces
Use magnification to distinguish particles from fungal structures
Keep affected lots identifiable through harvest
commonMistakes: Calling all pale surface material powdery mildew
Spraying water onto dense flowers without considering wetness risk
Mixing heavily exposed material into unaffected lots
Ignoring neighboring soil or road dust sources

title: Outdoor IPM, Beneficials & Edge Scouting
summary: Outdoor pest pressure is dynamic because crops are connected to surrounding vegetation and beneficial organisms. Edge scouting, organism identification, and population trends are more informative than reacting to every insect found on a plant.
keyConcepts: Crop edges can receive different pest pressure than interior plants
Predators, parasitoids, pollinators, and neutral arthropods should not all be treated as pests
Weather can rapidly change pest and beneficial populations
Damage level and population trend matter alongside presence
measureObserve: Scout edge and interior zones separately
Record pest and beneficial organisms
Inspect multiple life stages and damage patterns
Revisit hotspots after weather or management changes
commonMistakes: Treating all insects as harmful
Scouting only the easiest plants to reach
Applying a control before identifying the organism
Ignoring surrounding host vegetation

title: Rainfall, Irrigation & Water-Source Integration
summary: Outdoor irrigation should account for effective rainfall, root-zone storage, runoff, evapotranspirative demand, and source-water quality. Rainfall amount alone does not reveal how much water actually reached the active root zone.
keyConcepts: Rain can run off, evaporate, or wet only part of the root volume
Containers and raised beds respond differently from field soil
Source-water chemistry can change through the season
Repeated shallow irrigation can produce a different root distribution than deeper wetting
measureObserve: Use a rain gauge or reliable local precipitation record
Check moisture at root depth after rain
Track irrigation volume and distribution
Periodically characterize source water when it changes or symptoms suggest a need
commonMistakes: Skipping irrigation because rain occurred without checking root depth
Counting forecast rainfall as delivered water
Ignoring seasonal source-water changes
Watering only at the stem base as the root system expands

title: Topography, Microclimate & Cold-Air Drainage
summary: Slope, aspect, structures, vegetation, soil moisture, and cold-air movement can make nearby outdoor sites behave differently. Microclimate mapping helps explain repeated hot, humid, windy, or frost-prone zones.
keyConcepts: Cold dense air can settle in low areas during calm clear nights
South- and west-facing exposures can experience different heat loads than shaded aspects
Walls and fences can create both shelter and stagnant air
Vegetation alters shade, wind, humidity, and competition
measureObserve: Place temporary sensors in suspected hot and cold spots
Map slope and aspect
Record morning dew persistence
Compare wind exposure across the site
commonMistakes: Assuming one yard equals one microclimate
Placing the only sensor near a building
Ignoring cold-air drainage
Treating recurring location-specific stress as a cultivar problem
